prompt: Which ACID property guarantees a transfer doesn't debit without crediting?

options.text: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability

prompt: How does a database make committed data durable?

options.text: It keeps committed rows pinned in RAM until the next checkpoint
It writes to an on-disk write-ahead log before commit returns
It takes a full backup of the changed tables after each commit
It returns the written rows to the client to keep as a copy

explanation: The write-ahead log is flushed to disk before the commit is acknowledged, so it survives a crash and is replayed on restart. RAM is lost on a crash, per-commit backups would be far too slow, and clients don't hold the database's durable copy.

scenario: Two requests both run `SELECT stock` (10), compute 10 − 1 in code, then `UPDATE … SET stock = 9`. Two items sold, stock shows 9.

options.text: Dirty read
Non-repeatable read
Lost update
Phantom read

explanation: Both read 10, both wrote 9: one decrement vanished. An atomic `SET stock = stock - 1` fixes it.

prompt: Which anomaly is this, and which level prevents it?
scenario: Two managers each check 'at least one approver remains' (count = 2), then each removes themselves from approvers in separate rows, at Repeatable Read in Postgres. Zero approvers remain.

options.text: Lost update; Read Committed
Write skew; Serializable
Dirty read; Read Committed
Phantom; Read Uncommitted

explanation: Each transaction read the same rule and updated a different row: write skew. Snapshot isolation allows it; Serializable prevents it.

options.text: Reading another transaction's writes before it has committed
A repeated range query sees rows another transaction added or removed
Reading a row whose table was dropped while the query was running
Getting an old result from a cache instead of the current table

explanation: A phantom is about the set of rows matching a condition: re-running the range query returns rows another transaction inserted or deleted. Reading uncommitted data is a dirty read, and dropped tables and stale caches aren't isolation anomalies.

options.text: Reading another transaction's uncommitted writes
Reading a disk block that failed its checksum
Reading a value that changed since your last read
Reading a stale value from a cache in front of the DB

explanation: Dirty means uncommitted: you see writes that may yet be rolled back. A corrupted block is a storage fault, a value that changed between your reads is a non-repeatable read, and cache staleness is outside the database's isolation.

prompt: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level?

options.text: Read Uncommitted
Read Committed
Repeatable Read
Serializable

explanation: Postgres defaults to Read Committed; MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read.

prompt: What must your code do when using Serializable isolation?

options.text: Nothing extra, since the database queues conflicting transactions
Retry transactions that fail with serialisation errors
Disable indexes on hot tables so predicate locks stay small
Run every read at Read Uncommitted so writers aren't blocked

explanation: Serializable aborts conflicting transactions instead of letting anomalies through, so the application must catch serialisation failures and retry. It doesn't silently queue them, dropping indexes makes locking coarser, and mixing in Read Uncommitted reads defeats the guarantee.

prompt: What is the headline benefit of MVCC?

options.text: Tables stay smaller because each row keeps only its latest version
Readers don't block writers, and writers don't block readers
Version numbers on each row remove the need for most indexes
Row versions can be spread across nodes, giving free sharding

explanation: With MVCC each transaction reads its own snapshot of row versions, so reads and writes don't wait on each other. It actually keeps several versions (more space until VACUUM), still needs indexes, and has nothing to do with sharding.

scenario: A Postgres table that's updated 3,000 times a second has doubled in size today. A developer's session has had an open transaction since 9 a.m.

options.text: The disk is failing, so the same pages are written again and again
An open transaction's snapshot stops VACUUM removing old versions
Each update writes a duplicate index entry that is never removed
Writes are being lost and retried, so each row is inserted twice

explanation: Old row versions can't be reclaimed while any transaction might still need them, so a session open since 9 a.m. blocks VACUUM and dead versions pile up. A failing disk doesn't grow tables, index entries are cleaned up by VACUUM too once it can run, and lost writes would shrink data, not double it.

scenario: A booking system lets two guests book room 12 for the same night when they click at the same moment. Bookings are rows in `bookings(room, day, guest)`.

options.text: Use Read Uncommitted so each booking sees the other
A UNIQUE constraint on (room, day)
Cache room availability and check the cache first
Retry every failed booking until one finally wins

explanation: A unique constraint on (room, day) blocks the second insert at any isolation level. Read Uncommitted makes races worse, a cache adds another stale read before the same race, and retries don't stop two inserts that both succeed.
